html:
The grain domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from a wild grass called teosinte, and the staple food of most of the Americas before 1492. Today it is grown on every inhabited continent.

Early maize had cobs no longer than a finger. Over thousands of years farmers bred bigger cobs, and the crop spread north and south. It fed the maize-farming peoples of Mesoamerica and the Andes, and much later, around 900 CE, it became the base of town life in the Mississippi valley, alongside the older Eastern Agricultural Complex crops.

Native farmers worked out how to get the most from it:

  • Soaking it in lime or ash water (nixtamalisation) makes it more nourishing and easier to grind.
  • In three sisters fields, maize grows with beans and squash.
  • On the chinampas of the Valley of Mexico, raised beds gave several harvests a year.
  • The Inca kept it in state storehouses and brewed it into beer.

In the Maya Popol Vuh the gods make the first true people out of maize dough.

After 1492 maize went round the world in the Columbian exchange. It reached China in the 1500s and fed population growth in hill country, and became a staple across much of Africa and southern Europe.
